1.title: Edelzwicker: From "Zwicker" to "Noble Blend"
1.html:
"Zwicker" in the Alsatian dialect means "blend, mix". Historically, these different varieties were planted in the same field, and farmers were used to harvesting and vinifying them together. Later, to stress quality, farmers added "Edel" (meaning "noble") in front of "Zwicker", marking a shift in which specially selected quality varieties replaced simple high-yielding ones — this is the origin of the name "Edelzwicker".

Today Edelzwicker refers generally to any wine blended from Alsace white grape varieties, with proportions unrestricted and undisclosed, the varieties vinified separately or together, and the vintage label optional. The label does not (and may not) list variety names — one of the most direct differences from Gentil.
2.title: Gentil: The Modern Revival of a 1920s Tradition
2.html:
The concept of "Gentil" goes back to the 1920s: at that time many plots were planted with a mix of varieties, and farmers were used to harvesting and vinifying them together — in fact in line with what some Alsace Clos (such as Zahnacker) preserve today.

In recent years, the old term Gentil has been redefined and regulated by the trade charter (Charte Interprofessionnelle) and become the exclusive term for a "quality blended wine". The rules require:

  • In the blend, at least 50% must come from the four noble varieties Riesling, Muscat, Pinot Gris and Gewurztraminer
  • The remainder may be made up with Sylvaner, Chasselas or Pinot Blanc
  • Each variety must first be vinified separately and obtain AOC Alsace approval before the final blending
  • After blending and bottling, the wine must also pass a tasting approval (dégustation d'agrément) before it can be officially sold
3.title: Edelzwicker vs Gentil at a Glance
3.items.0.desc: A blend of any Alsace white grape varieties, with proportions unrestricted and undisclosed, no variety names on the label, the representative everyday table wine — fresh and easy to drink, with no need for ageing, suited to salads and light cold dishes.
3.items.1.desc: A "quality blended wine" governed by the trade charter: ≥50% noble varieties plus complementary varieties, each vinified separately and approved before blending, and it must pass a post-bottling tasting approval before sale — a higher-end version able to accompany a whole meal.
4.question: What is the main difference in winemaking process between Gentil and Edelzwicker?
4.options.0: Gentil can be made from only a single variety
4.options.1: Gentil requires each variety to be vinified separately and obtain AOC Alsace approval before the final blend, and after bottling it must also pass a tasting approval before sale
4.options.2: Edelzwicker needs more than 10 years of ageing
4.options.3: The winemaking process of the two is exactly the same
4.explanation: Gentil is governed by the trade charter: each variety must first be vinified separately and obtain AOC Alsace approval before the final blend, and after the blend is bottled it must also pass a tasting approval (dégustation d'agrément) before it can be officially sold — this whole rigorous process is Gentil's quality guarantee as a "quality blended wine", and the most fundamental difference from Edelzwicker, which may be blended freely and needs no approval.
5.keyPoints.0: Edelzwicker: from the dialect "Zwicker" (blend) + "Edel" (noble), freely blended, no varieties on the label
5.keyPoints.1: Gentil: goes back to a 1920s tradition, recently re-regulated and revived by the trade charter
5.keyPoints.2: Gentil requires ≥50% noble varieties, each vinified separately and approved, and a post-bottling tasting approval
5.keyPoints.3: The two represent two different positionings of Alsace blended wine: the "everyday" and the "quality" tier
